title: Algebra I — Common Core High School Math — Answer Key
id_format: S<set>-<section>-Q<number>; section is M (main), B1, B2, ... (backward), F1 or F2 (forward)
grading_rules: Match each student response to its key record by the question ID printed on the question page (for example S40-F2-Q3). The page number is the same in the Question Collection and the Answer Key. IDs are unique within one grade's collection; across collections use uid (for example G5:S40-F2-Q3).
Multiple choice and true/false: the response is correct when the chosen letter equals correct_letter, or when the student wrote the text of the correct choice.

Short answer: accept any mathematically equivalent form unless the question asks for a specific form (equivalent fractions, decimals, and mixed numbers; a ratio written as a : b, a to b, or a/b; "x = 5" or "5"; terms of an expression in any order). Units are not required unless the question asks for them.
When an answer has several parts (separated by semicolons, or with labels such as "Rate of change:"), every part must be correct.
Drawing / plotting questions (type plot): correct_answer describes what a correct drawing shows. Judge the student's drawing against it.

Drawing + written questions (type plot_text): the student draws on the figure AND writes an answer. drawing_answer describes the correct drawing and correct_answer the written answer. Both must be correct: every requested point, segment or shape in the drawing, and the written conclusion.

Answer with required work (type work): required_method says what the shown work must use. A correct final answer without that work earns partial credit only; correct work with a slip in the final answer is also partial.
Explain / describe questions: grading_note says what a correct response must include; accept any reasonable wording.
grading_note also lists other accepted answers and the work behind an answer. It is guidance for the grader, not for students.

Algebra I answer forms: the grading_note of every written answer begins with "Form required:" or "Any equivalent form". When a form is required (for example expanded, factored completely, simplest radical form, slope-intercept form, vertex form, exact value, or a stated rounding), an answer in another form is not full credit even if it is equivalent.

Equations, inequalities, and systems: "x = 3" and "3" are the same answer; a solution set must contain every solution (both roots of a quadratic, in any order); "no solution" and "all real numbers" are answers when the key says so; an inequality may be written either way round (x > 2 or 2 < x) unless a notation is asked for; a solution of a system may be written as an ordered pair or as x = ..., y = ....
Every question has an explanation in its grading_note, after the form rule. It shows why the key is correct and can be shown to the student as feedback after grading.

questions.set_title: Explain the meaning of rational exponents from the properties of integer exponents

questions.set_title: Explain why sums and products of rational and irrational numbers are rational or irrational
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.domain: Number & Quantity: The Real Number System
questions.question: Explain why 5 + √2 is irrational. (Suppose 5 + √2 = r for some rational number r.)
questions.required_method: An argument like this: if 5 + √2 = r with r rational, then √2 = r - 5, a difference of rational numbers, which is rational. But √2 is irrational, so 5 + √2 cannot be rational.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form of the argument. The key step is that rational numbers are closed under subtraction.

questions.set_title: Explain why sums and products of rational and irrational numbers are rational or irrational
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.domain: Number & Quantity: The Real Number System
questions.question: Explain why 3√7 is irrational. (Suppose 3√7 = r for some rational number r.)
questions.required_method: An argument like this: if 3√7 = r, then √7 = r ÷ 3, a quotient of a rational number by a nonzero rational number, which is rational. But √7 is irrational, so 3√7 is irrational.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form of the argument. It uses closure of the rational numbers under division by a nonzero number.

questions.set_title: Explain why sums and products of rational and irrational numbers are rational or irrational
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.domain: Number & Quantity: The Real Number System
questions.question: Explain why the sum of two rational numbers a/b and c/d (with integers a, b, c, d, and b ≠ 0, d ≠ 0) is rational.
questions.correct_answer: a/b + c/d = (ad + bc)/(bd). ad + bc and bd are integers and bd ≠ 0, so the sum is a quotient of integers.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation that writes the sum as a quotient of integers with a nonzero denominator.

questions.question: A car goes 32 miles on each gallon of gas, and gas costs $3.60 per gallon. Use units to find the cost of gas for a 400-mile trip.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. 400 miles × (1 gallon ÷ 32 miles) × ($3.60 ÷ 1 gallon) = $45; the miles and gallons cancel.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: Convert 72 kilometers per hour to meters per second.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. 72 km/h × 1,000 m/km ÷ 3,600 s/h = 20 m/s.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: The formula d = rt gives distance. A rate r is in meters per second and a time t is in minutes. What must be done before multiplying?

choices.text: Convert t to seconds (or r to meters per minute).

questions.correct_answer: Convert t to seconds (or r to meters per minute).
questions.grading_note: The time units must match: (m/s) × s = m.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: A graph will show a town's population each year from 1990 to 2020. The populations range from 12,000 to 31,000. Choose a scale for the vertical axis, and explain your choice.
questions.correct_answer: For example, 0 to 35,000 in steps of 5,000, labeled "Population"; every value fits and the steps are equal.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form: any labeled scale with equal steps that includes 12,000 to 31,000 (starting at 10,000 instead of 0 is also correct if the break is shown or stated).

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: A speed of 5 miles per hour is about 7.3 feet per second.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Convert measurement units with ratio reasoning
questions.question: How many inches are in 3.5 feet?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. 3.5 × 12 = 42.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Convert measurement units with ratio reasoning
questions.question: How many kilograms are in 2,500 grams?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. 2,500 ÷ 1,000 = 2.5.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Convert measurement units with ratio reasoning
questions.question: How many feet are in 4 yards?
questions.grading_note: 1 yard = 3 feet, so 4 yards = 12 feet.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Convert measurement units with ratio reasoning
questions.question: 1 hour = 3,600 seconds
questions.grading_note: 60 minutes × 60 seconds = 3,600 seconds.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Convert measurement units with ratio reasoning
questions.question: 5 km = 500 m

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Compute unit rates with fractions
questions.question: A walker goes 3/4 mile in 1/4 hour. How many miles per hour is this?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. (3/4) ÷ (1/4) = 3.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Compute unit rates with fractions
questions.question: Half a pound of cheese costs $3. What is the price per pound?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. $3 ÷ (1/2) = $6.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Compute unit rates with fractions
questions.question: 2/3 gallon of paint covers 1/3 of a fence. How many gallons cover the whole fence?
questions.grading_note: (2/3) ÷ (1/3) = 2 gallons per fence.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Compute unit rates with fractions
questions.question: Walking 1/2 mile in 1/6 hour is a speed of 3 miles per hour.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Compute unit rates with fractions
questions.question: Painting 1/4 of a wall in 1/2 hour is a rate of 1/8 wall per hour.
questions.grading_note: (1/4) ÷ (1/2) = 1/2 wall per hour.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Use density in a model
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Copper has a density of 8.96 grams per cubic centimeter. What is the mass of a 5 cubic-centimeter piece of copper?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. Mass = density × volume = 8.96 × 5.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Use density in a model
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A county has 240,000 people living in 600 square miles. What is its population density?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form, with units. 240,000 ÷ 600 = 400.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Use density in a model
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A 2 cm by 3 cm by 4 cm block has a mass of 60 grams. What is its density?
questions.grading_note: The volume is 24 cubic centimeters, and 60 ÷ 24 = 2.5.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Use density in a model
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Population density is the number of people divided by the area they live on.
questions.grading_note: Density is a quantity per unit of area (or volume).

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Use density in a model
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: An object with a volume of 10 cubic centimeters and a density of 3 grams per cubic centimeter has a mass of 3.3 grams.
questions.grading_note: Mass = 3 × 10 = 30 grams.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Solve problems with velocity vectors
questions.grade: High School — Precalculus (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A boat heads east at 12 km/h across a river whose current flows north at 5 km/h. What is the boat's resulting speed?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. The velocities are perpendicular, so the speed is √(12² + 5²) = 13.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Solve problems with velocity vectors
questions.grade: High School — Precalculus (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A plane points north at 300 km/h, and the wind blows west at 40 km/h. Write its velocity as (east part, north part) in km/h.
questions.grading_note: Form required: (east part, north part). West is the negative east direction.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Solve problems with velocity vectors
questions.grade: High School — Precalculus (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Two velocities, (3, 4) and (5, -1), are added. What is the result?

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Solve problems with velocity vectors
questions.grade: High School — Precalculus (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: An object with velocity (6, 8) meters per second has a speed of 10 meters per second.

questions.set_title: Use units to guide multistep solutions and to choose scales for graphs
questions.section_title: Solve problems with velocity vectors
questions.grade: High School — Precalculus (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Adding the velocities (3, 0) and (0, 4) gives a speed of 7.
questions.grading_note: The sum is (3, 4), whose speed is √(9 + 16) = 5.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: A school wants to model the total cost of a field trip by bus. Name the quantities the model needs, with a unit for each.
questions.correct_answer: The number of students (students), the students each bus holds (students per bus), the cost of each bus (dollars per bus), and the admission price (dollars per student).
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form: any complete, sensible set of quantities, each with a unit.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: A club rents a room for $300 and pays $40 for each member who attends. Its cost model is C = 40n + 300. Define C and n, with units.
questions.correct_answer: C is the total cost in dollars; n is the number of members who attend.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent wording, with both units.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: Which quantity best describes how fast a phone battery runs down?

choices.text: Number of apps on the phone
Width of the screen in inches
Mass of the phone in grams
Percent of charge used per hour

questions.correct_answer: Percent of charge used per hour
questions.grading_note: A rate of drain needs an amount of charge per unit of time.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: Two towns have different populations and different areas. Define one quantity, with units, that compares how crowded they are.
questions.correct_answer: Population density: people per square mile (or per square kilometer).
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent quantity that is people per unit of area.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: Kilowatt-hours per month is a sensible quantity for a model of a household's electricity use.
questions.grading_note: It measures energy used per unit of time, which is what an electricity bill is based on.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Use variables to represent quantities in a situation
questions.question: Tickets cost $8 each. Write an expression for the cost of n tickets.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Use variables to represent quantities in a situation
questions.question: A worker earns $15 per hour plus a $20 bonus. Write an expression for the pay for h hours.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Use variables to represent quantities in a situation
questions.question: A typist types 30 words per minute. Which expression gives the number of words typed in m minutes?
questions.grading_note: Words = rate × time = 30m.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Use variables to represent quantities in a situation
questions.question: If w is a number of weeks, 7w is the number of days.
questions.grading_note: Each week has 7 days.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Use variables to represent quantities in a situation
questions.question: If d is a number of dollars, d + 5 is 5 times as many dollars.
questions.grading_note: 5 times as many is 5d; d + 5 is 5 more.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Write and solve px + q = r from a word problem
questions.question: A gym charges a $25 fee plus $10 per class. Tom paid $95. How many classes did he take?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. 25 + 10c = 95 gives c = 7.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Write and solve px + q = r from a word problem
questions.question: A phone costs $50 plus $15 per month. The total so far is $140. For how many months has it been paid?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. 50 + 15m = 140 gives m = 6.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Write and solve px + q = r from a word problem
questions.question: A plumber charges a $12 fee plus r dollars per hour. A 3-hour job costs $57. Which equation fits?
questions.grading_note: 3 hours at r dollars is 3r, plus the $12 fee.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Write and solve px + q = r from a word problem
questions.question: x = 6 is the solution of 4x + 6 = 30.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Write and solve px + q = r from a word problem
questions.question: x = 3 is the solution of 2x - 5 = 11.
questions.grading_note: 2 · 3 - 5 = 1; the solution is x = 8.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Use geometric quantities to make design decisions
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A rectangular garden needs an area of at least 200 square feet and can use at most 60 feet of fence. Does a 10 ft by 20 ft garden meet both requirements? Explain.
questions.correct_answer: Yes. Its area is 200 square feet and its perimeter is 60 feet.
questions.grading_note: Both checks are required.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Use geometric quantities to make design decisions
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A box with a square base 10 cm on each side must hold 1,000 cubic centimeters. How tall must it be?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. 10 × 10 × h = 1,000.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Use geometric quantities to make design decisions
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A rectangular pen must have an area of 100 square meters. Which dimensions use the least fence?
questions.grading_note: The perimeters are 40, 50, 58, and 104 meters.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Use geometric quantities to make design decisions
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A 6 by 6 square has more area than a 4 by 8 rectangle, even though their perimeters are equal.
questions.grading_note: 36 > 32, and both perimeters are 24.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Use geometric quantities to make design decisions
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Of all rectangles with a perimeter of 20, the 1 by 9 rectangle has the greatest area.
questions.grading_note: Its area is 9; the 5 by 5 square has area 25.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Recognize surveys, experiments, and observational studies and the variables they measure
questions.grade: High School — Probability & Statistics (course placement in this bank)
questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.question: A researcher randomly assigns 40 plants to two fertilizers and measures each plant's growth in centimeters. What kind of study is this, and what is the response variable (with units)?
questions.correct_answer: An experiment; the response is growth in centimeters.
questions.grading_note: Both parts are required.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Recognize surveys, experiments, and observational studies and the variables they measure
questions.grade: High School — Probability & Statistics (course placement in this bank)
questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.question: A survey asks 200 randomly chosen students how many hours they sleep on a school night. What kind of study is this, and what variable does it measure?
questions.correct_answer: A survey (sample survey); hours of sleep per school night.
questions.grading_note: Both parts are required.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Recognize surveys, experiments, and observational studies and the variables they measure
questions.grade: High School — Probability & Statistics (course placement in this bank)
questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.question: Which kind of study can show cause and effect?
questions.grading_note: Only random assignment of treatments controls for other variables.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Recognize surveys, experiments, and observational studies and the variables they measure
questions.grade: High School — Probability & Statistics (course placement in this bank)
questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.question: In an observational study, the researchers do not assign treatments.
questions.grading_note: They observe groups that already exist.

questions.set_title: Define appropriate quantities for descriptive modeling
questions.section_title: Recognize surveys, experiments, and observational studies and the variables they measure
questions.grade: High School — Probability & Statistics (course placement in this bank)
questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.question: A survey of volunteers who answer an online poll is a random sample.
questions.grading_note: Volunteers choose themselves, so the sample is not random.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: A ruler measures to the nearest 0.1 cm. A rectangle measures 4.3 cm by 2.7 cm, and a calculator gives its area as 11.61 square cm. Which report of the area best fits the accuracy of the measurements?
questions.grading_note: Each length could be off by 0.05 cm, so the true area is between about 11.3 and 12.0 square cm; the hundredths digit is not known.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: A stopwatch reads to the nearest 0.1 second. A runner covers 100 m in 12.4 seconds, and a calculator gives 8.0645161 meters per second. Report the speed to a sensible accuracy.
questions.grading_note: Form required: a rounded value. 8.1 or 8.06 m/s is accepted; the true speed is between about 8.03 and 8.10 m/s, so more digits are not meaningful.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: A tape measure is marked in centimeters. Which is the most sensible report of a person's height measured with it?
questions.grading_note: The tape measures to the nearest centimeter, so report whole centimeters.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: A bridge is 1,250 m long, measured to the nearest 10 m. Between which two lengths is its true length?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. Measuring to the nearest 10 m allows an error of up to 5 m either way.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Algebra I main question
questions.question: Giving more decimal places always makes a measured answer more accurate.
questions.grading_note: A result cannot be more accurate than the measurements it comes from.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Estimate to check whether an answer is reasonable
questions.question: Estimate. 4.9 × 21.2
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent estimate near 100: 5 × 20 = 100.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Estimate to check whether an answer is reasonable
questions.question: Is 38.4 ÷ 4.8 = 80 reasonable? Explain.
questions.correct_answer: No. 40 ÷ 5 = 8, so the answer should be about 8.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Estimate to check whether an answer is reasonable
questions.question: Which is the best estimate of 19.8% of 503?
questions.grading_note: About 20% of 500 is 100.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Estimate to check whether an answer is reasonable
questions.question: $29.95 × 4 is about $120.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Estimate to check whether an answer is reasonable
questions.question: 0.48 × 61 is about 300.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Round decimals to any place
questions.question: Round 8.0645 to the nearest hundredth.
questions.grading_note: Form required: hundredths. The thousandths digit is 4, so round down.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Round decimals to any place
questions.question: Round 11.61 to the nearest whole number.
questions.grading_note: Form required: a whole number. The tenths digit is 6, so round up.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Round decimals to any place
questions.question: Round 0.0357 to the nearest thousandth.
questions.grading_note: The ten-thousandths digit is 7, so round up.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Round decimals to any place
questions.question: 3.149 rounded to the nearest tenth is 3.1.
questions.grading_note: The hundredths digit is 4, so round down.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Round decimals to any place
questions.question: 6.95 rounded to the nearest tenth is 6.9.
questions.grading_note: The hundredths digit is 5, so round up to 7.0.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Use volume formulas and report results to a sensible accuracy
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A cylinder has a radius of 3.0 cm and a height of 10.0 cm. Find its volume to the nearest cubic centimeter.
questions.grading_note: Form required: rounded to the nearest whole number. V = π · 3² · 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Use volume formulas and report results to a sensible accuracy
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A sphere has a radius of 5 m. Find its volume exactly in terms of π, then to the nearest cubic meter.
questions.grading_note: Form required: both the exact and the rounded value. V = (4/3)π · 125.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Use volume formulas and report results to a sensible accuracy
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A cone has a radius of 6 and a height of 4. What is its volume?

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Use volume formulas and report results to a sensible accuracy
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: A cube with 2 cm edges has a volume of 8 cubic centimeters.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Use volume formulas and report results to a sensible accuracy
questions.grade: High School — Geometry (course placement in this bank)
questions.question: Doubling the radius of a sphere doubles its volume.
questions.grading_note: Volume depends on r³, so it is multiplied by 8.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Use the margin of error of a sample survey
questions.grade: High School — Probability & Statistics (course placement in this bank)
questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.question: A poll reports that 54% of voters support a plan, with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. What interval of values for the true percent does this give?
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent form. 54% - 3% to 54% + 3%.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Use the margin of error of a sample survey
questions.grade: High School — Probability & Statistics (course placement in this bank)
questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.question: A poll reports 54% support with a margin of error of 3 percentage points. Do the results suggest that a majority supports the plan? Explain.
questions.correct_answer: Yes. Every value in the interval, 51% to 57%, is above 50%.
questions.grading_note: Any equivalent explanation that uses the interval.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Use the margin of error of a sample survey
questions.grade: High School — Probability & Statistics (course placement in this bank)
questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.question: A poll reports 48% support with a margin of error of 4 percentage points. Which statement fits?

choices.text: Fewer than half support the plan, for certain.
The true percent could be above or below 50%.

questions.correct_answer: The true percent could be above or below 50%.
questions.grading_note: The interval 44% to 52% includes values on both sides of 50%.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Use the margin of error of a sample survey
questions.grade: High School — Probability & Statistics (course placement in this bank)
questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.question: Larger random samples tend to have smaller margins of error.
questions.grading_note: More data gives less variation from sample to sample.

questions.set_title: Choose a level of accuracy that fits the limits of measurement
questions.section_title: Use the margin of error of a sample survey
questions.grade: High School — Probability & Statistics (course placement in this bank)
questions.domain: Statistics & Probability: Making Inferences & Justifying Conclusions
questions.question: A margin of error of 3 percentage points means the poll is off by exactly 3 points.
questions.grading_note: It gives a range of plausible values, not the exact error.
